$comment: Maestro's own MCP tool surface, served by `maestro-server mcp` (see mcp_stdio.rs). Descriptions are the ONLY documentation the agent receives — the skill no longer ships the canvas catalog — so prose here is behaviour, not commentary. `{components}` in a description is replaced at load with the pretty-printed `components` section of canvas-catalog.json. Adding a tool here also needs an arm in the host's `host_tools::handle`, or the gateway will forward calls nobody answers.

tools.name: canvas_create
tools.description: Open a canvas surface in Maestro's side panel. Always the first call for a new surfaceId, before canvas_data or canvas_update. Reuse one surfaceId for a whole answer — a new surface per tool call produces disconnected panels. Never narrate these calls to the user; they see the rendered surface, not the machinery.

surfaceId.description: Your identifier for this surface; reuse it in every later call.

tools.name: canvas_data
tools.description: Store data on a surface at a JSON Pointer path, for Chart and DataTable to bind to. Call this BEFORE the canvas_update that references the path — a component pointing at an empty path shows a skeleton forever. DataTable rows are positional arrays of cells indexed by column order, not objects keyed by column key.

tools.name: canvas_update
tools.description:
Add or update components on a surface. Components are a flat adjacency list: each has an `id` and a `component` type, and nests by listing child ids in `children`. Re-sending a component with the same id updates it in place, so a dashboard can fill in while tool calls run.

Order is canvas_create, then canvas_data, then canvas_update.

Controls (Button, TextField, CheckBox, ChoicePicker, Slider, DateTimeInput) report back only while a canvas_await is pending. Outside that window the user can still fill them in, and nothing is sent to you — which is the right shape for a UI mock. Component ids are scoped to their surface, so two forms may both use `branch` without colliding.

Component props:
{components}

tools.name: canvas_await
tools.description: Wait for the user to act on a surface's controls, and return what they did. This is what makes the controls answer — render the form with canvas_update first, then call this. Returns `{event:{surfaceId,componentId,kind,value,values}}`, where `values` holds every field on that surface, so one form is one round trip. Omit `surfaceId` to take whichever canvas the user acts on: they can page between every surface you have drawn, and the event names the one they used. Pass `surfaceId` only to insist on a particular canvas — one that does not match a canvas you created waits for nothing. Returns `{timeout:true}` if nothing happened in the window; call again to keep waiting.

surfaceId.description: Restrict the wait to one surface. Omit to accept any.

tools.name: create_task
tools.description: Create a Maestro task in the Planning column of the current project. Use when the user asks for work to be tracked, or when you find follow-up work worth recording. The task is created immediately — say what you created and quote the id.

description.description: Markdown. What needs doing and why.

tools.name: list_tasks
tools.description: List the current project's tasks, newest first. Archived tasks are excluded. Use it to check whether work is already tracked before creating a task.
